did_you_know.text: The Babylonian siege of Jerusalem began on the tenth day of the tenth month, in the ninth year of Zedekiah’s reign. The Babylonian army surrounded the city and built a siege ramp around it to cut the city off and pressure it to surrender.
The siege continued until Zedekiah’s eleventh year. By then, the famine in the city had become so severe that there was no bread left for the common people.
When the city was breached, the soldiers went out at night through a gate between the two walls, near the king’s garden, and tried to escape toward the Arabah.
Zedekiah was captured in the plains of Jericho after the Chaldean army pursued him. His soldiers scattered, and he was brought to the king of Babylon at Riblah for judgment.
The punishment pronounced against Zedekiah had two recorded stages: his sons were killed before his eyes, and then he was blinded and taken to Babylon in bronze chains.

In the fifth month, in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuzaradan arrived in Jerusalem. He burned the Lord’s temple, the king’s palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem, while the Babylonian army tore down the city walls.
Not all the people of the land were exiled. Nebuzaradan left behind the poorest of the people, including vinedressers and farmers—people who could continue working the land.

The chapter gives a detailed account of the bronze items taken from the temple, including the two pillars, the bronze Sea, and the stands. It says that there was so much bronze that the weight of all the items could not be determined.

After the destruction, the king of Babylon appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, over the people who remained in Judah. Gedaliah encouraged them to stay in the land and serve the king of Babylon so that things would go well for them.

At the end of the chapter, thirty-seven years after Jehoiachin was taken into exile, Evil-merodach king of Babylon released him from prison, gave him an honored position, and provided him with a regular meal every day.
